opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from realizing that the absence of something in your immediate surroundings doesn't mean it doesn't exist. Early on, there were stretches where I didn't have a mentor who really understood what I wanted to do, or I'd meet investors or interviewers who were judging things in ways that felt a bit shallow. It would have been easy to conclude, "Well, this is just how the world works." But I don't think that's the right lesson.

The way I see it, the people around you at any given moment are a very small sample. If you only have access to a few people, it's statistically pretty likely that none of them is the perfect match for you. That says more about the size of your network than about whether good mentors exist. So I try to hold on to the belief that somewhere there's someone who will look at your work carefully, understand the reasoning behind it, and give you honest, useful feedback.

That belief changes how you act. If you assume good judges exist, you focus on doing work that would hold up under a thoughtful person's scrutiny, instead of optimizing for whoever happens to be in front of you. You keep putting your work out there, writing it up, open-sourcing it, reaching out, because you expect that eventually it'll reach someone who gets it. And in my experience, that does happen. Often the people who end up mattering most come from places you didn't expect.

There's also a practical side: if you believe good mentors and evaluators are rare or don't exist, you become cynical, and cynicism makes you stop trying in subtle ways. Believing they exist keeps you honest with yourself. It pushes you to become the kind of person who would earn their respect, and over time you also start trying to be that mentor or that fair interviewer for others. So even when I couldn't see them around me, believing in them was what kept me moving in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker expects eventually to reach someone who understands their work, but it does not say that person shares the speaker’s belief in good people.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes from a few moments where someone did show up for me when they had no reason to, and once you've seen that happen even once, you can't un-see it.

When I was a student, I wasn't the obvious candidate for anything. I wasn't from the famous lab, I didn't have the pedigree. And there were people, a professor who answered a cold email, an engineer who spent an hour on a call with me when he had nothing to gain, who treated me as if I was already the person I was trying to become. That changes you. It's not that they handed me opportunities. It's that they made me believe the opportunity existed, and that there were people on the other side of it who were actually looking for someone like me.

So when people say, "there's nobody like that around me," I understand the feeling, but I think the framing is slightly wrong. Good mentors and good investors are rare, yes, but they're not uniformly distributed. They tend to be busy, they tend to be in places you're not yet, and they tend to respond to signal. So the question isn't whether they exist, it's whether you've given them a reason to find you. When I started working on open-source projects, I wasn't trying to find a mentor. I was just trying to make something work. But the work itself became the thing that connected me to people I would never have met otherwise. Code is a very honest introduction.

And I'd say the same about interviewers. People talk about interviews as adversarial, like the person across the table is trying to catch you. In my experience, most good interviewers genuinely want you to succeed. They're bored of saying no. They want to find the person who's going to make their team better. If you walk in assuming that, you behave differently. You explain your thinking instead of hiding it. You admit what you don't know. And that's exactly what a good interviewer is looking for.

So believing in them is partly a strategy. If you assume the good ones are out there, you keep putting work into the world, you keep reaching out, you keep being honest in rooms where it would be easier to perform. And that behavior is what eventually puts you in front of them. If you assume they don't exist, you stop doing the things that would let them find you, and then your belief becomes self-fulfilling.

I'd also add, and this is maybe the part I feel most strongly about, that once you've benefited from someone like that, you have an obligation to become that person for someone else. There's a version of the world where the good mentor around you is just you, a few years from now, and the fastest way to make sure there are good people around is to be one.

r001.rationale: The response says assuming good mentors exist and continuing to put work into the world can eventually put you in front of them. It does not say that someone you meet will share your belief.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to believe that someone could recognize the value of what you’re doing, even if you haven’t met that person yet. Otherwise, it’s easy to let the people immediately around you define what’s possible for you.

A good mentor might see potential you haven’t learned to express. A good investor might understand an idea before it becomes obvious. A good interviewer might give you the chance to show how you think. Believing those people exist doesn’t mean expecting someone to rescue you. It means continuing to prepare, to explain yourself more clearly, and to look for the right people instead of treating every rejection as a final judgment.

r001.rationale: The response encourages believing that good mentors, investors, and interviewers exist and continuing to look for them, but it does not assert that the speaker will eventually meet someone who shares that belief.

sol-6.1.text:
I think believing that good mentors, investors, and interviewers exist keeps you open to finding them. If you assume everyone will misunderstand you or judge you unfairly, you might stop reaching out before you meet someone who really gets what you’re trying to do.

That doesn’t mean trusting everyone blindly. You can be selective and learn from disappointing experiences without deciding that every future experience will be the same. And you can ask yourself: What would a good mentor challenge me to think about? What would a thoughtful investor need to understand? Those questions help you prepare, even before that person shows up.

So for me, it’s a useful kind of optimism. You keep improving, keep looking, and give people the chance to surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response says belief can keep someone open to finding good mentors and gives people a chance to surprise them, but it does not assert that they will eventually meet someone who shares that belief.
